items.t: Case law — inspector's dismissal quashed for not carrying the 'severe' highways finding into the planning balance (Greystoke)
items.b: In Greystoke CB Ltd v Secretary of State for Housing, Communities and Local Government [2026] EWHC 1997 (Admin) the Planning Court quashed an inspector's decision dismissing an appeal for a large (about 140,000 sq m) employment development near Junction 11 of the M40 in Oxfordshire. Coppel J held that, having found the residual highway impacts would not be 'severe', the inspector erred by not applying that conclusion at the planning-balance stage, and remitted the appeal for redetermination.

items.t: Case law — challenge to China embassy planning permission and listed building consent dismissed (Royal Mint Court)
items.b: In R (Royal Mint Court Residents' Association) v Secretary of State for Housing, Communities and Local Government [2026] EWHC 2002 (Admin) a Divisional Court dismissed a statutory challenge to the Secretary of State's grant of planning permission and listed building consent for the People's Republic of China's embassy at Royal Mint Court, London. All grounds failed, so the consents stand.

items.t: GPDO amended — domestic solar equipment permitted development revised (SI 2026/896)
items.b: The Town and Country Planning (General Permitted Development) (England) (Amendment) Order 2026 (SI 2026/896) was made on 29 July 2026, laid before Parliament on 30 July and comes into force on 27 August 2026 in England. It amends Part 14 of the GPDO 2015, revising the permitted development rights for installing or altering solar equipment on domestic premises (Class A) and stand-alone solar equipment within a dwellinghouse curtilage (Class B), with transitional provision. Verify before relying.

items.t: Case law — warehouse permission challenge dismissed (Upper Nene SPA)
items.b: In R (Staunch Campaign Ltd) v North Northamptonshire Council [2026] EWHC 1962 (Admin) the Planning Court dismissed a judicial review of permission for around 185,000 m2 of B8 warehousing on greenfield land near Titchmarsh. The claimant argued the Habitats Regulations Assessment mishandled effects on the Upper Nene Valley Gravel Pits Special Protection Area; Sir Peter Lane rejected all five grounds, holding the council lawfully treated replacement functionally linked land as mitigation and was entitled to rely on Natural England's advice.

items.t: Case law — suspended prison term for breach of planning injunction (Maidstone)
items.b: In Maidstone Borough Council v Fred King [2026] EWHC 1965 (KB) the High Court found the defendant in contempt for breaching orders prohibiting residential caravan and mobile-home use of agricultural land at Sandway. Mr Justice Griffiths imposed a six-month custodial sentence suspended on condition the site is cleared and the orders complied with by January 2027, underlining the courts' willingness to commit for persistent planning enforcement breaches.

items.t: Case law — Tottenham Hotspur Whitewebbs Park permission quashed (Enfield)
items.b: In R (Guardians of Whitewebbs Park CIC) v London Borough of Enfield [2026] EWHC 1916 (Admin) the Planning Court quashed Enfield's grant of planning permission for a Tottenham Hotspur women's and girls' training academy on Green Belt land at Whitewebbs Park. The court found the officers' report seriously misrepresented the council ecology officer's advice — reporting 'no objection' when he in fact disputed the developer's claimed biodiversity net gain figure — and that failing to publish his report as a background paper under s.100D of the Local Government Act 1972 caused material prejudice to objectors.

items.t: Neighbourhood planning toolkits — five new MHCLG guides added
items.b: MHCLG added five new toolkits to its neighbourhood planning collection on 24 July 2026: making Local Green Space designations, addressing regeneration in a neighbourhood plan, establishing a neighbourhood forum, and two on consulting environment statutory consultees (a template consultation form and a worked example). They are non-statutory guidance to help communities in England prepare and consult on neighbourhood plans.

items.t: BNG reform — new exemptions and revised hierarchy from 6 August (SI 2026/790)
items.b: The Biodiversity Gain (Town and Country Planning) (Amendments and Transitional Provisions) (England) Regulations 2026 (SI 2026/790) were laid before Parliament on 13 July 2026 and take effect on 6 August 2026 in England. They add a new exemption for development affecting under 0.2 hectares of onsite habitat (unless priority habitat is affected) and for temporary development reinstated within five years, revise the biodiversity gain hierarchy for non-major development, and remove the self-build and custom build exemption. The changes apply to applications made on or after 6 August 2026; applications already submitted remain under the existing BNG rules. Verify before relying.

items.t: NSIP pre-application consultation requirement removed from 24 July
items.b: From 24 July 2026 the statutory requirement for mandatory pre-application consultation on Nationally Significant Infrastructure Projects is removed in England under the Planning and Infrastructure Act 2025. MHCLG says applicants will instead receive earlier technical advice from the Planning Inspectorate, with new pre-application guidance replacing the statutory consultation stage; the government estimates the change could cut up to 12 months from NSIP timelines.

items.t: Case law — challenge to West Suffolk Local Plan dismissed
items.b: In Lochailort Kentford Ltd v West Suffolk Council [2026] EWHC 1870 (Admin) the Planning Court dismissed a challenge to adoption of the West Suffolk Local Plan. The claimant argued that adding part of its promoted site to the Brownfield Land Register after the examination closed showed the site was suitable, contradicting the council's case for rejecting it; the court found no inconsistency or irrationality and indicated it would in any event have withheld relief under the Simplex principle.

items.t: National scheme of delegation for planning decisions (SI 2026/854)
items.b: The Town and Country Planning (Discharge of Local Planning Authority Functions) (England) Regulations 2026 were made and published on 21 July 2026 and come into force on 31 October 2026 in England. They introduce a national scheme of delegation: Schedule 1 applications (including householder, minor residential and commercial, permission in principle and certain lawful development certificates) must be decided by officers, while Schedule 2 applications (including listed building consent, reserved matters and applications the authority considers significant) may go to committee. Applications in which the authority has an interest go to committee, and committee sizes are capped. Verify before relying.

items.t: Case law — 45° daylight rule must be applied, not just cited
items.b: In R (Manby) v Hackney [2026] EWHC 1543 (Admin) the Planning Court quashed a householder permission because the officer's report recited the council's 45-degree daylight rule but never applied it — no assessment, calculation or site visit. The court found a failure to have regard to a material consideration, a breach of the Tameside duty and inadequate reasoning.
